output.headline: Investigation into Channel dinghy incident leads to Daniel Thomas’s arrest
output.bodyHtml:
Police have arrested the far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas on suspicion of “criminal damage with intent to endanger life”, after he filmed himself appearing to slash the side of a dinghy in the middle of the Channel while a rescuer was onboard.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said a 37-year-old man, of no fixed abode, had been arrested after a boat carrying an emergency responder was damaged in the Channel. The man was arrested “on suspicion of destroying ships or fixed platforms or endangering their safety”.

Police said he remained in custody on Thursday, also suspected of committing “criminal damage, criminal damage with intent to endanger life, and conduct endangering ships, structures or individuals”.

The force said it had been examining footage livestreamed by Thomas, which reportedly appears to show him using a knife to stab and slash an inflatable dinghy in the middle of the Channel after asylum seekers had been helped to safety, but with a French rescue worker who had just got onboard.

Thomas’s footage appeared to show him approaching one of the dinghies, which was empty, shouting: “Let’s get rid of that boat.” After the rescue worker got onboard, Thomas shouted: “Get off the boat. You’ve got time to get off the boat.” The footage then shows Thomas’s boat speeding away before the rescue worker climbed back on the larger boat.

More than 200,000 people watched the livestreamed footage, in which Thomas, who goes by the name Danny Tommo, filmed himself from a boat as he spent the afternoon tracking two dinghies carrying asylum seekers from France to the UK.

Thomas, a longtime associate of fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, AKA Tommy Robinson, had repeatedly told his followers they should march silently, without violence, and avoid doing anything that could lead to arrests. This summer he gathered dozens of nationalist protest groups under the umbrella anti-immigration movement Patriot Platform, which was behind marches this month in Dover and Portsmouth, when masked men in black gathered and protested over immigration and asylum policy.

A police officer is seen, in a 56-second clip uploaded to Thomas’s YouTube platform on Wednesday night, telling him he was being arrested on suspicion of criminal damage “recklessly endangering someone’s life” — footage Thomas apparently managed to film and upload before police were able to stop him.

Thomas said: “I understand. I knew this was coming.”

Most small boats carrying asylum seekers across to the UK are escorted to shore by rescue services or Border Force vessels, and no unescorted small boats had been recorded since 6 September 2025 — until two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days brought renewed focus on the Home Office’s handling of small-boat arrivals, amid which Thomas’s arrest came.

A total of 21 people were detained after a boat evaded Border Force to reach the beach of Samphire Hoe in Dover on Wednesday, a second uncontrolled landing after another dinghy reached Folkestone on Monday morning, prompting the education secretary, Lucy Powell, to say: “You can’t stop everything all of the time”.

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has responded by ordering an urgent review by Border Security Command, after describing the failure to intercept the two boats as “not acceptable”.

Powell, speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, said: “Of course, it’s a concern. That’s why the home secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable.”
output.standfirst: Daniel Thomas, 37, is being held on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life after footage appeared to show him slashing a dinghy in the Channel with a rescue worker onboard

output.headline: Andy Burnham's Labour draws progressive voters back as tactical voting reshapes the race, poll finds
output.bodyHtml:
Labour could come within touching distance of a majority at the next election, a major poll has found, if tactical voting proves as widespread as progressive voters suggest – a shift that would also push Reform UK into fourth place.

Andy Burnham is drawing a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, the results suggest, motivated by a wish to stop Nigel Farage.

The poll of more than 8,000 voters, shared with the Guardian, shows the prime minister’s most successful electoral strategy would be to unite the centre and left bloc of voters while the right remains split, and suggests a widespread openness to voting tactically.

The approach marks a shift from the tactics of Keir Starmer’s Labour before the 2024 general election, when the party sought to attract more conservative older voters instead. Some in Labour may be unsettled by the parallel, since the same strategy was used for Ed Miliband’s failed bid in 2015, albeit before Reform’s arrival as a major electoral force.

Related: From idealists to struggling sceptics: how Labour’s majority depends on five progressive voter types – in charts

Conducted on the eve of Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool, the poll shows a significant shift of left-leaning voters towards Burnham’s Labour, encouraging those in the party weighing an early election while Reform’s ratings ebb and leftwing parties such as the Greens appear to be losing momentum.

Since April, twice as many voters have returned to Labour from the left as from the right.

Survation and the progressive activist site 38 Degrees carried out the previously unreleased research, including a seat-by-seat MRP model, during Burnham’s first month as prime minister.

Labour would be the largest party in parliament if an election took place today, the poll suggests, winning 272 seats – a four-point lead worth 42% of parliamentary seats from 28% of the vote.

Reform would become the official opposition on 153 seats, representing 24% of seats – the same as its vote share – while the Conservatives would fall to third place with 85.

A far higher share of voters in the tightest marginals say they are open to voting tactically when asked to name their preferred party – a sign of how fluid the polls remain. Two hundred seats are decided by under five points in total, meaning a two- to three-point swing could move about 100 seats likely to decide a future election.

Labour and the Conservatives would benefit if voters switch to one of the two frontrunners in their seats rather than their preferred party – a shift that would cut Reform UK’s seat count dramatically.

About 18% of voters in seats where tactical voting would make a substantial difference say they are willing to switch but have not yet done so; if they did, Reform UK would be reduced to 62 seats and Labour would rise to 319 – six short of a majority.

Of the 91 seats where Reform would cease to be the most likely winner, 46 would go to the Conservatives and 43 to Labour, though the projection is unlikely to be exact at this stage in the electoral cycle.

In 59 seats – among them the Wrekin, Torridge and Tavistock, and North West Cambridgeshire – Reform’s chances of winning fell by more than 50 points; all three have Reform as the most likely leader under the “normal” assumptions but lose out to the Conservatives once more tactical voting is factored in.

The base modelling of the MRP gives Reform a 51% chance of winning a tight race in Rawmarsh and Conisbrough, but that falls sharply once tactical voting increases, with a 76% chance of Labour holding the seat instead. In 2024, the now-chancellor, John Healey, held the seat with 49% of the vote, with Reform in second place on 28.6%.

In Bassetlaw, tactical voting would lift Labour’s vote share from 32% to 40%, enough that the forecast winner shifts from Reform, with a 77% chance, to Labour, with a 58% chance – even though Reform’s own vote share also rises, from 35% to 40%. The Conservatives, Liberal Democrats and Greens would lose supporters if this switching took place.

Newark, held by the Conservative-turned-Reform MP Robert Jenrick, is forecast to flip to the Conservatives under both scenarios; heavier tactical voting would lift the chance of a Conservative win from 68% to more than 99% should Labour backers vote Conservative to stop him.

Damian Lyons Lowe, Survation’s chief executive, said: “Estimating tactical voting is a complex consideration, but the mechanics here are simple. Four in 10 voters are currently backing a party that can’t finish in the top two where they live and are willing to vote tactically.

“But when we ask whether they would lend their vote to the stronger local contender in a two-horse race, around half said yes. That gap – worth some 18 points of the national electorate – is an enormous untapped reservoir for parties looking to squeeze voters.

“Should these voters act as they say, our model shows Reform falling from second place to fourth, losing around 90 seats, despite its own vote share actually going up. Reform-leaning Conservatives will consolidate too. Reform doesn’t collapse; it risks being outnumbered, seat by seat, by voters coordinating around whoever is best placed locally on the left and right.”

Progressive voters living in seats such as Labour-held Southend would be unlikely to switch to the Conservatives even if they were technically best placed to beat Reform at the next election, which shows the limits of predictions around tactical voting – a limitation sharpened by the sheer number of seats Labour won in 2024 from the Conservatives where the party has been polling as low as third over the past year.

Labour is also gaining considerable numbers of voters back from other leftwing parties, though not from Reform, the poll suggests. The share of Labour’s lost 2024 voters going to the Greens, Liberal Democrats, Plaid Cymru or the Scottish National party has fallen from 60% to 46%; on the right, the share lost to Reform or the Tories has fallen from 27% to 24%.

Veronica Hawking, the campaigns director at 38 Degrees, said the polling pointed to a far more optimistic public mood than before the Labour conference last year, alongside significant expectation that Burnham needed to deliver.

“There are signs of optimism and even hope, but what has not changed is the way voters are crying out for bold action, fast,” she said. “The results show a huge amount of common ground between voters, especially when it comes to the cost of living. Voters who have moved in different directions since the general election two years ago are united by the fact that action on the cost of living crisis will have the single biggest bearing on their future vote.”
output.standfirst:
Andy Burnham is drawing progressive voters back to Labour to stop Nigel Farage, a poll of more than 8,000 people finds, with tactical voting potentially pushing Reform UK into fourth place

output.headline: Rail unions call for more staff and policing as reported assaults hit record high
output.bodyHtml:
Unions are calling for more staff and policing on Britain’s railways after reported assaults rose to a record high of almost 25,000 incidents in a year.

The ‘horrendous’ figures, according to unions, come as the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) reported a sharp increase in assaults on the travelling public and on railway staff last year.

Reported assaults against passengers and other members of the public on the mainline railway reached 13,464 in 2025-26, up 36 per cent on the previous year and the highest number recorded by the ORR since it began tracking the figures in 2004.

Assaults on rail staff rose 12 per cent in a year to 11,289 reported incidents, mainly verbal abuse but including nearly 2,500 physical assaults, an average of about seven a day.

Assaults on members of the public included sharp rises in cases of harassment, up 52 per cent year on year, and common assault, up 30 per cent.

The figures partly reflect increased reporting and zero-tolerance campaigns on public transport, though they also underline concerns raised by unions about the ongoing threats facing frontline workers as well as passengers, and the availability of transport police.

The RMT general secretary, Eddie Dempsey, said the numbers were horrendous but matched the union’s own surveys showing two-thirds of its members had experienced some form of violence at work in the past year.

He said: ‘We are calling for a significant increase in staffing across public transport, including an end to lone working. We also clearly need stronger legal protections for public transport workers against assaults at work.

‘British Transport Police funding cuts have also been disastrous which has undermined a proper policing presence on all public transport.’

The chief inspector of railways, the ORR’s Richard Hines, said: ‘The increase in reported assaults is concerning. No one on the railway should be subjected to violence, threats or abuse.

‘We’re working with industry and our trade union colleagues to address work-related violence and harassment, including through recent guidance which sets out what we expect from rail employers.

‘This includes understanding where the risks are, putting effective controls in place, encouraging staff to report incidents and providing appropriate support afterwards. Our inspectors will continue to check how these risks are being managed.’

A spokesperson for Network Rail and train operators said: ‘Violence, abuse and intimidation directed at passengers or staff are completely unacceptable. The rail industry works closely with British Transport Police to investigate incidents, support victims and bring offenders to justice.’

They said the numbers also reflected greater intelligence sharing, improved reporting processes, and more CCTV and body-worn cameras for frontline staff.

On the London Underground, where assaults on the workforce are counted individually rather than by incident, the number fell slightly last year. The ORR report noted that the national headline numbers can include multiple counts in a single incident, for example for both harassment and common assault, while workforce assaults are now recorded even if no physical injury occurs.

The chief executive of the Rail Safety and Standards Board, Mark Phillips, said the rail industry was taking action to better protect staff, but the figures ‘underline the need for a change in public behaviour and greater respect for the people who keep the railway running safely every day’.

Reports in recent years have highlighted that women and girls were at particular risk, while the growing number of assaults year on year since the pandemic has coincided with pressure on British Transport Police numbers.

The abuse and intimidation faced by frontline staff on the railways has also been seen in sectors including retail and in the NHS. The British Retail Consortium warned over ‘endemic’ violence towards shop workers earlier this year, while the number of reports of violence against NHS staff by patients surpassed 100,000 in 2025.

The Department for Transport and British Transport Police were approached for comment.
output.standfirst:
Reported assaults on Britain’s railways rose to a record high of almost 25,000 in the past year, figures unions call ‘horrendous’ and say show the need for more staff and policing

output.headline: Treasury insists budget will stay ‘focused’ despite bond sell-off driving up UK borrowing costs
output.bodyHtml:
John Healey faces a tough budget next month, with a global sell-off in government bonds having put fresh upward pressure on UK borrowing costs.

The yield – effectively the interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds, known as gilts, stood at 5.38% by mid-morning on Thursday, nearing the 19-year high reached last week.

Higher interest rates raise the upfront cost of government investment and feed through into Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts of whether the chancellor is on course to meet Labour’s fiscal rules.

Analysts believe the recent rise in yields has wiped out more than half of the £24bn “headroom” against the rules that the former chancellor Rachel Reeves had built up at the time of the spring statement in March.

Related: The perilous economic conditions facing the UK can be traced back to Trump | Richard Partington

Healey, her successor, has repeatedly pledged to meet the rules while keeping a “buffer against uncertainty”, though this buffer is widely expected to be significantly lower than £24bn.

Treasury sources insist the budget will be “focused”, with important spending decisions postponed to a review next year, even though rebuilding the buffer to its previous level would be likely to require large tax increases or spending cuts.

Investors across the main markets have been ditching bonds in recent weeks in a wave of selling prompted by fears of higher inflation and interest rates as the conflict in the Middle East rumbles on.

The Bank of England’s chief economist, Clare Lombardelli, set out in a speech on Thursday the conditions that would shape UK interest rates, saying that the longer oil prices remained elevated as a result of the war, the more likely it was that rates would have to rise.

“The longer higher energy prices persist, the greater the risk that indirect effects build and that inflation expectations, wage bargaining and price-setting behaviour begin to adjust in response,” she told an economic conference in Warsaw, Poland.

“On that basis, policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation or weaker activity.”

Andy Burnham’s government has promised to offer consumers a “breathing space” against the rising cost of living, at a time when higher rates would mean increased mortgage costs for homeowners.

The Bank is also forecasting a sharp, 24% rise in the quarterly energy price cap that determines household utility bills in January, if oil prices remain high.

Lombardelli’s message echoed that of the Bank governor, Andrew Bailey, after the nine-member monetary policy committee left interest rates on hold at 3.75% last week.

She stressed that high oil prices had had less impact on other prices across the economy than the Bank had feared; but the longer they remained high, the greater the risk of inflation becoming entrenched.

The bond sell-off continued on Thursday, with yields on 30-year US Treasury bonds rising to 5.444% – the highest level since 2004.

Investors also appear concerned about the risks of uncontrolled US government spending, alongside higher inflation; some analysts suggest large-scale bond issuance by AI firms is also undermining demand for treasuries.
output.standfirst:
The rising cost of the 10-year gilt, nearing a 19-year high, is pushing up the upfront cost of government investment and narrowing chancellor John Healey’s room for manoeuvre ahead of next month’s budget

  • Business live – latest updates

  • International bodies warn of rising debt and borrowing risks

  • Burnham stands by claim UK is ‘in hock’ to bond markets

output.headline: Newcastle University faces questions over sustainability professorship for Indian oil heir
output.bodyHtml:
Conservationists have questioned Newcastle University’s decision to appoint the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune, who also runs a controversial mega-zoo, as a professor of sustainability.

Anant Ambani was given the professorship of practice, the university said, for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.

Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who built his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and maintains close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.

Ambani, 31, leads renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn. He has also set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly houses more than 150,000 animals, including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.

Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing, though conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals, many of them endangered species, were sourced.

Academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists reacted to the university’s announcement with incredulity and derision.

Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.

“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”

Bhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator into illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”

Prof Matt Perry, the chair of the University and College Union branch at Newcastle University, said staff members had objected to the appointment citing environmental concerns.

Prof Lyla Mehta, the head of the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.

She said: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”

In April, Anant Ambani launched Vantara University, described as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.

Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”

An investigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung found, in 2025, that many animals delivered to Vantara had arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been trafficked illegally.

India’s supreme court investigated the zoo’s operators and cleared them of any wrongdoing, in an inquiry, in August last year, that lasted less than three weeks. A subsequent fact-finding mission into the zoo by Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were probably forged.

Its report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”

Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals, though it later reversed the decision after India, the US and Japan objected at a Cites meeting, arguing there was not enough proof of illegal imports.

In August, the zoo launched a “reset” of its operations, appointing a former Cites head to oversee them and pledging to pause all wildlife imports voluntarily until June next year.

The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking, saying: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.” Vantara declined to comment for this article.

A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”
output.standfirst: Academics and conservationists have reacted with incredulity to Newcastle’s award for Anant Ambani, son of India’s richest person, who also runs a controversial mega-zoo

output.headline: US and China extend Busan trade truce to January as Trump gives Xi rare welcome to Washington
output.bodyHtml:
Donald Trump personally welcomed Xi Jinping to the US, taking the unusual step of greeting the Chinese leader on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews to open his state visit to Washington.

US service members lined a 30-metre-long (100ft) red carpet for the lavish ceremony that greeted Xi’s plane, which also included a military flyover by two B-1 bombers and a presentation of the flags and national anthems of both countries.

Trump and the first lady, Melania, travelled to the military base in Maryland, just outside Washington, on Wednesday evening to personally shake hands with Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan – a departure from the usual practice of presidents welcoming foreign leaders at the White House.

Related: AI looms large over Trump-Xi meeting amid deep distrust between US and China

World leaders are gathering in New York for the United Nations general assembly at the same time as Xi’s visit, though the Chinese leader will not address the meeting – he has attended the UNGA only once since becoming president in 2012.

Richard Gowan of the International Crisis Group told Reuters: “It’s pretty notable that Xi Jinping is ⁠coming to Washington in the same week as the general assembly, but does not feel bothered to come up to New York. I think a lot of people will say: ‘Where is the real center of decision-making?’”

The US and China agreed on Wednesday to extend the so-called Busan agreement, a temporary trade truce between the world’s two biggest economies, Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, announced.

Bessent, who met the Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng earlier on Wednesday, told Fox News the agreement would run until 10 January, two months beyond its original expiry.

A formal state welcome on the South Lawn of the White House, private tea with the president and first lady, and a tour of the National Archives are among the events still to come in the pageantry surrounding the visit.

During the two-day visit, Trump and Xi must also confront a number of thorny issues, including the race in artificial intelligence development, geopolitical instability and the simmering trade war.

Executives from OpenAI, Apple, xAI, Microsoft, Nvidia, Meta and other major tech companies have been invited by the White House to a state dinner being held for Xi on Thursday.

The one unscripted moment in the carefully orchestrated arrival ceremony came when a US military jet flew overhead as Trump and Xi stood on the red carpet listening to the US national anthem: video of the moment showed Xi remaining impassive, as did the wives of both men, while Trump visibly winced and recoiled at the sound of the flyover.

Widely mocked online, the moment was captured on a White House livestream, though it was not included in the edited highlights of the ceremony that Trump’s aides released later.

The US and China have long been competing on technology in general, but the race to advance AI in particular has become a major topic among tech companies, especially after several executives came forward to warn about the dangers of rapid development.

Trump has promoted more investment in the technology so the US can beat China in the race, having dismissed concerns that AI development could harm people.

Trump wrote on Truth Social last week: “There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS! We are leading China, and all others, and will continue to do so,”

The president and members of his administration have argued that leading in AI also means leading the world militarily and economically, raising the stakes further for both the US and China.

The ceremonial displays expected throughout Xi’s visit reciprocate the treatment Trump received when he visited China earlier this year.

By choosing to greet the Chinese leader at his plane rather than at the White House, Trump signalled how far he is willing to go to honour Xi.

“He’s coming on our soil,” Melania Trump said of the visit, speaking to Fox & Friends on Wednesday morning, “and we need to welcome them with the most respect.”

Robert Mackey contributed reporting
output.standfirst:
Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said the ‘Busan agreement’ truce would run until 10 January, as Trump personally welcomed Xi at Joint Base Andrews with a red carpet and military flyover.
